mainTopic: Who owns the ground under sold trees: a seller who keeps the trees or the land, the dispute of רבי עקיבא and רבנן, trees planted too close together, and the buyer of a date palm.
overview: This amud first finishes explaining why someone who sells land but keeps his trees surely kept the ground they stand on: otherwise the buyer could make him uproot them. It then turns to the reverse case, where someone sells trees and keeps the land. That case depends on the dispute between רבי עקיבא, who says a seller sells generously, and רבנן, who say he sells sparingly. The גמרא shows that each side still fits the earlier rulings of רב זביד and רב פפא, because those rulings were about two separate buyers. Next, the נהרדעי say that eating the fruit of crowded trees gives no חזקה. רבא challenges this from an alfalfa field and moves the rule to a sale: a buyer of crowded trees gets no land. רבי זירא ties this to a dispute of תנאים about a crowded vineyard. The amud closes with a new ruling of the נהרדעי: a buyer of a date palm owns from its base down to the depths.

steps.title: A seller who keeps his trees surely kept the ground under them
steps.stepSummary: When someone sells land but keeps the trees, he certainly kept the ground for them. If he had not, the buyer could tell him to uproot his tree and leave.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the trees drain strength from the land, the seller surely kept the ground for them. If he had not kept it, the buyer could say to him: 'Uproot your tree and go.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its reasoning about a person who sold his land but kept the trees for himself. It concludes that he surely held on to the ground the trees need.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Trees pull nutrients from the soil, so they take something away from the buyer's land. If the seller had not kept the ground, the buyer could force him to remove the trees altogether. Since the seller clearly meant to keep his trees standing, he must have meant to keep their ground too.

phrases.english: since they drain the land,
he certainly kept [the ground] for himself.
For if he had not kept it,
let [the buyer] say to him:
Uproot the tree and go.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the reasoning, begun before this section, about a seller who keeps his trees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A seller who keeps his trees surely kept the ground under them.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Because the trees harm the land and the buyer could otherwise demand that they be uprooted, the seller must have kept their ground.

steps.title: Selling trees but keeping the land depends on רבי עקיבא and רבנן
steps.stepSummary: In the reverse case, where someone sells trees and keeps the land, the law depends on the dispute between רבי עקיבא and רבנן. רבי עקיבא gives the buyer the ground under the trees; רבנן do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone sold trees and kept the land for himself, this depends on the dispute between רבי עקיבא and רבנן. According to רבי עקיבא, who says a seller sells generously, the buyer gets the ground. According to רבנן, he does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the opposite case: now the trees are sold and the land is kept. It ties the answer to a known dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the buyer is the one who wants the ground, so nothing points clearly in his favor. The answer depends on our general view of sellers. If they sell generously (רבי עקיבא), the ground is included; if they sell sparingly (רבנן), it is not.

keyTerms.meaning: a seller sells generously (with a 'good eye')
he has it / he does not have it

steps.confusionAlert: This is the reverse of step 1. There the seller kept the trees; here the seller sold the trees and kept the land. Do not mix up who is the buyer.

phrases.english: If he sold trees and kept the land for himself,
it is the dispute of Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis.
According to Rabbi Akiva, who says:
a seller sells generously,
[the buyer] has [the ground under the trees];
according to the Rabbis, he does not have it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the case of a seller who keeps the trees to the reverse case of a seller who keeps the land.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A buyer of trees gets the ground under them according to רבי עקיבא, but not according to רבנן.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא's view still works even for רב זביד
steps.stepSummary: Even רב זביד, who said the tree owner gets no land, would agree with רבי עקיבא here. His ruling was about two buyers; here a seller is dealing with one buyer, and a seller sells generously.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבי עקיבא the buyer has the ground, and this holds even according to רב זביד, who said the tree owner has none. That was only about two buyers, where the land buyer can say: 'Just as I have nothing in the trees, you have nothing in the land.' But here a seller sells generously.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא heads off a possible question: doesn't רב זביד's earlier ruling contradict רבי עקיבא's view? It explains that the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב זביד ruled about two separate buyers, one of the land and one of the trees. They stand as equals, so each can say the other gets only what he bought. With a seller and his buyer, רבי עקיבא's rule that a seller sells generously applies, so the ground goes to the buyer.

phrases.english: According to Rabbi Akiva, he has [the ground],

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲפִילּוּ לְרַב זְבִיד דְּאָמַר: אֵין לוֹ –
phrases.english: and even according to Rav Zevid, who said: he has none,
phrases.notes: This points back to רב זביד's ruling on the previous page, where one person got the land and another got the trees.

phrases.english: that applies only to two buyers,
since [the land buyer] can say to him:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דִּלְדִידִי לֵית לִי בְּאִילָנוֹת,
phrases.english: Just as I have nothing in the trees,
you too have nothing in the land;
but here,
a seller sells generously.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲפִילּוּ לְרַב זְבִיד דְּאָמַר: אֵין לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how רבי עקיבא's side of step 2 fits with רב זביד's earlier ruling.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Separating the cases: two equal buyers versus a seller and one buyer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think רב זביד's 'he has none' would also deny the land to a buyer of trees under רבי עקיבא.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב זביד spoke only about two buyers. With a seller, רבי עקיבא's generous-seller rule gives the buyer the ground.

steps.title: רבנן's view still works even for רב פפא
steps.stepSummary: Even רב פפא, who said the tree owner does get land, would agree with רבנן here. His ruling was about two buyers who each claim equal generosity; here a seller sells sparingly.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבנן the buyer does not have the ground, and this holds even according to רב פפא, who said the tree owner does have it. That was only about two buyers, where the tree buyer can say: 'Just as he sold to you generously, he also sold to me generously.' But here a seller sells sparingly.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the mirror image of step 3. The גמרא shows that רב פפא's earlier ruling does not contradict the view of רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With two buyers, the tree buyer can demand equal treatment: the seller was generous to the land buyer, so he must have been generous to the tree buyer too. When the seller keeps the land himself, there is no second buyer to compare with. So רבנן's rule that a seller sells sparingly holds, and the seller keeps the ground.
steps.whatToRemember: The two-buyer rulings of רב זביד and רב פפא do not decide the seller-and-buyer case. When a seller keeps the land, it all depends on whether sellers sell generously (רבי עקיבא) or sparingly (רבנן).

phrases.english: According to the Rabbis, he does not have [the ground],

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲפִילּוּ לְרַב פָּפָּא דְּאָמַר: יֵשׁ לוֹ –
phrases.english: and even according to Rav Pappa, who said: he has it,
that applies only to two buyers,
since [the tree buyer] can say to him:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דִּלְדִידָךְ זַבֵּין בְּעַיִן יָפָה,
phrases.english: Just as he sold to you generously,
he also sold to me generously;
but here,
a seller sells sparingly.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲפִילּוּ לְרַב פָּפָּא דְּאָמַר: יֵשׁ לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The parallel to step 3, this time for the view of רבנן and the ruling of רב פפא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Separating the cases: two equal buyers versus a seller and one buyer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think רב פפא's 'he has it' would give the buyer of trees the ground even under רבנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב פפא's reasoning rests on equal treatment between two buyers. With a seller, רבנן's sparing-seller rule leaves the ground with the seller.

steps.title: Eating fruit of crowded trees gives no חזקה
steps.stepSummary: The נהרדעי rule that if someone ate the fruit of trees planted too close together, he does not gain a חזקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages of נהרדעא say: if a person ate the fruit of trees that were planted crowded together, he does not get a חזקה on them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from the נהרדעי about trees that are planted too close together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, eating the fruit of a field for the required time gives a person a חזקה, which is a presumption of ownership. The נהרדעי say this does not work when the trees are crowded, so eating that fruit proves nothing. This sets up רבא's challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages of the city נהרדעא
A presumption of ownership that comes from using the land
He ate them, meaning he ate their fruit

phrases.english: The Sages of נהרדעא say:
If he ate their fruit when they were crowded together,
he does not have a חזקה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about trees planted too close together.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating the fruit of crowded trees does not give a חזקה.

steps.title: רבא asks: then how does anyone own an alfalfa field?
steps.stepSummary: רבא objects: an alfalfa field is always planted densely, so under this rule nobody could ever gain a חזקה on one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא challenges this: if that is true, then how does a person ever acquire an alfalfa field?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the ruling of the נהרדעי by pointing to an alfalfa field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An alfalfa field is planted thickly by its nature, yet people obviously own such fields by using them. If crowded planting stopped a חזקה, a person could never gain a חזקה on an alfalfa field. That result makes no sense, so the ruling of the נהרדעי cannot stand as stated.

keyTerms.meaning: He objects to it, he challenges it
If so, then (introduces a strange result of the ruling)
Alfalfa, a crop that grows thickly

phrases.english: Rava objects to this:
If that is so,
this field of alfalfa,
phrases.notes: Alfalfa always grows packed tightly together, so a field of it is always "crowded."

phrases.english: with what does one acquire it?

steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling of the נהרדעי that eating crowded trees' fruit gives no חזקה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An alfalfa field is always crowded, yet it can be owned through use. So crowding cannot be what blocks a חזקה.

steps.title: רבא restates the rule: crowded trees sold, buyer gets no land
steps.stepSummary: רבא moves the rule from חזקה to a sale: if someone sells crowded trees, the buyer does not get the land around them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: if he sold trees that are crowded together, the buyer has no land.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the first version failed, רבא gives a new version of the rule that applies to a sale instead of a חזקה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Crowding does not stop a חזקה, as the alfalfa field shows. But it does matter when trees are sold: a buyer of crowded trees does not get the ground with them. So the crowding rule is kept, just moved to a different case.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, he said (replaces the earlier version)

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not just saying the נהרדעי were wrong. He keeps the idea that crowding matters, but applies it to buying land in a sale, not to a חזקה.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
If he sold them when they were crowded together,
he has no land.
phrases.notes: "He" here is the buyer. He gets the trees, but not the ground around them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 by restating the rule in a new case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rewording the original statement so it applies to a different case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Crowded trees block a חזקה from eating their fruit.
steps.terutzMaskana: Crowded trees do not block a חזקה; they only mean a buyer of the trees does not get the land.

steps.title: רבי זירא: this matches a dispute about a crowded vineyard
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא says רבא's rule depends on a dispute of תנאים about a vineyard planted with less than four אמות between vines.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: this is like a dispute of תנאים. A vineyard planted with less than four אמות between the vines: רבי שמעון says it is not a vineyard. The חכמים say it is a vineyard, and we look at the middle vines as if they are not there.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא shows that רבא's rule about crowded trees matches one side of an older dispute between תנאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון says a crowded vineyard does not count as a vineyard, which fits רבא: crowded trees are not a real orchard, so no land comes with them. The חכמים ignore the middle vines, so the outer ones still form a proper vineyard. By that view, crowded trees could still count as an orchard and the buyer would get land.

keyTerms.meaning: Four אמות, the normal spacing between rows of vines
We view them as if they are not there

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's rule (crowded trees sold, no land) fits רבי שמעון. By the חכמים, the middle trees are ignored, so the group can still count as an orchard.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said: This is like a dispute between Tannaim:
phrases.notes: "This" is רבא's rule from the step before, about selling crowded trees.

phrases.english: A vineyard that is planted
with less than four cubits between the vines,
Rabbi Shimon says: It is not a vineyard.
And the Rabbis say: This is a vineyard,
and we view the middle vines as if they are not there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ties רבא's rule from step 7 to a dispute between תנאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא's rule matches רבי שמעון, who says crowded plantings do not count. The חכמים ignore the middle plants and still count it.

steps.title: Selling a date palm: the buyer owns from its base down to the depths
steps.stepSummary: The נהרדעי rule that someone who buys a date palm acquires it from its base all the way down into the depths.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages of נהרדעא say: when someone sells a date palm to his friend, the buyer acquires it from its base down to the depths.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from the נהרדעי about buying a single date palm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even when a person buys only one tree, his rights do not stop at ground level. The buyer acquires from the bottom of the tree all the way down into the depths of the earth below it.

phrases.english: The Sages of Neharde'a say:
This one who sells a date palm to his friend,
the buyer acquires from its bottom until the depths.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי נְהַרְדָּעֵי: הַאי מַאן דְּזָבֵין דִּקְלָא לְחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ruling about selling a single tree.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A buyer of a date palm acquires from its base down to the depths.
